name: Choi implanter pen
lead: The Choi implanter pen is a hand-held device used in hair transplantation to make the recipient-site opening and place a harvested follicular unit in a single step. People choose it, typically as part of Direct Hair Implantation (DHI), to restore a hairline and density, with clinics saying the pen gives control over the angle, direction and depth of each graft so the result looks natural [1].

DHI is described as a variant of follicular unit extraction (FUE), in which grafts are loaded into the pen rather than placed into pre-cut slits [1]. FUE itself involves removing individual follicular units of one to four hairs with small punches under local anesthesia, leaving small punctate scars and a recovery of under a week, according to Wikipedia [2].

Reference sources describe the pen approach as typically more expensive and slower than conventional FUE, with fewer grafts per session and results that depend heavily on the surgeon [1]. The Wikipedia article on hair transplantation does not discuss the pen itself, and no controlled trial comparing pen implantation with other placement methods was identified [2].

paras: In pen-based implantation, individual follicular units are extracted by FUE and then loaded into a hollow needle-tipped pen. The surgeon uses the pen to open the recipient site and deposit the graft in one motion, so no separate slits are made in advance.[1]

Hair transplantation has two main harvesting methods. In strip harvesting (FUT) a strip of scalp about 1 to 1.5 by 15 to 30 cm is removed from the back of the scalp and dissected into grafts, leaving a thin linear scar that is usually covered by hair [2]. In FUE, individual follicular units are removed with 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches; it leaves small punctate scars, takes longer and costs more, and some surgeons report a lower ratio of successfully transplanted follicles than strip harvesting [2]. Pen-based implantation is a way of placing FUE-harvested grafts.

Wikipedia lists milestones in the field: Menahem Hodara's 1897 transplant onto scars, Norman Orentreich's late-1950s donor-graft experiments, the shift from plugs to strip excision in the 1980s, a 2002 publication on FUE by Rassman and colleagues, and FDA approval of the NeoGraft in 2009 and the ARTAS system in 2011 [2].

Proponents cite precise control of angle and depth for natural-looking hairlines and reported graft survival above 90 to 95 percent because handling time is short.[1] Listed drawbacks are higher cost, long sessions (6 to 10 hours is cited), dependence on operator skill and fewer grafts per session.[1] These figures come from a general reference page rather than from published trials.

Wikipedia reports temporary thinning of transplanted hair, called shock loss, is common after hair transplantation, and that alcohol and smoking have been cited as contributors to poor graft survival [2]. These points apply to hair transplantation in general rather than to the pen specifically.

timeline.event: Menahem Hodara transplants hair onto scars left by favus [2].
Rassman and colleagues publish on follicular unit extraction [2].
NeoGraft becomes the first FDA-approved robotic hair restoration device [2].
The ARTAS System receives FDA approval [2].

card.summary: A pen-style implanter that places each graft as the incision is made; clinics promote it, but published comparisons are absent.
card.note: Claims about survival and density come from clinics and general references, not trials.

quick.overview:
The Choi implanter pen is a tool used in some hair transplants to open the recipient site and insert a follicular unit in one step. It is the basis of the technique often marketed as DHI.

Clinics say it gives better control of angle and depth. Reference sources also note higher cost, longer procedures and fewer grafts per session.
quick.mechanism: Follicular units are extracted individually (FUE), loaded into the hollow pen, and implanted directly without pre-made slits.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE hair transplantation generally, such as swelling, folliculitis, scarring and poor graft take. No trials were found comparing the pen with other implantation methods.

chain: Follicular units are extracted by FUE
Pen opens the site and places each graft in one motion
Grafts grow as a natural-looking hairline and fuller density
angle.text: The pen is a transplant tool: it places the surgeon's harvested hairs into thinning or bald areas to rebuild a hairline or add density. Clinics offering it say the angle and depth control helps produce a natural-looking result.
